title: Complexity and Big-O Notation
tagline: Input size, dominant term, best/average/worst case, and the Big-O analysis of searching and sorting algorithms.

overview.intro: Complexity and Big-O notation are about how the work of an algorithm grows as the input gets larger. This chapter explains input size and the dominant term, introduces Big-O notation in simple terms, and discusses best, average and worst case. It then applies these ideas to searching and sorting, so you can see why some algorithms scale much better than others.

blocks.text: Complexity is the study of how the running time or the amount of work of an algorithm grows as the input gets larger. The main reason to study it is that a program that is fast enough for a small input can become far too slow for a large input if the algorithm is poorly chosen. Two programs that produce the same result are not equally good if one does ten steps and the other does ten million steps for the same size of input.

Complexity does not usually depend on the exact speed of a particular computer. Instead, it is about the pattern of growth. A good complexity analysis tells you how the work changes when the input size doubles, triples or grows much larger. That is why complexity matters even before you measure actual running time on a real machine. It helps you choose algorithms that will still be acceptable when the input grows.

learn.title: Input size and the dominant term

blocks.text: To analyse complexity, you first decide what counts as the input size. For a list, it is often the number of elements. For an n by n table, it might be n squared. Once you know the input size, you look at how many basic steps the algorithm takes. If the total number of steps can be written as an expression, the dominant term is the part that grows fastest as the input size increases. Smaller terms and constant factors matter less for large inputs.

That is why complexity analysis usually drops constant factors. An algorithm that takes 2n steps and one that takes 100n steps both grow in the same basic pattern, which is proportional to n. A constant factor can matter in practice, but for growth comparison the shape of the expression matters more than the exact multiplier. This is the idea behind Big-O notation: it describes the dominant part of the growth.

items.note: If an algorithm looks at each element once, its work often grows roughly like n.
If an algorithm compares every pair of elements, its work often grows roughly like n squared.

blocks.text: Big-O notation is a way of describing the upper growth behaviour of an algorithm in a simple form. When we say an algorithm is O of n, we mean its work grows at most like a constant times n for large inputs, ignoring smaller terms and constants. Big-O is not usually a statement about a single exact count of steps. It is a statement about the broad pattern of growth.

The common Big-O classes you are likely to meet are O of 1, O of n, O of n squared, and sometimes O of log n. O of 1 means constant time: the work does not depend much on the input size. O of n means the work grows roughly in proportion to the input size. O of n squared means the work grows like the square of the input size, which becomes expensive quickly. The exact formal definition is not the main point here; the patterns are.

items: Big-O describes a broad growth pattern.
O of 1 is constant time.
O of n grows roughly with the input size.
O of n squared grows like the square of the input size.
O of log n grows slowly as the input grows.

blocks.text: An algorithm can behave differently depending on the particular input it receives. The best case is the input that makes it do the least work. The worst case is the input that makes it do the most work. The average case is what happens on typical inputs. In many situations, the worst case matters most, because you want to know the maximum amount of work an algorithm might do.

For example, a simple search through an unsorted list may find the target immediately if it is at the very beginning, but it may have to check every element if the target is at the end or missing. That means the same algorithm can have very different work depending on the input. When people talk about complexity, they often mean the worst-case growth, unless they say otherwise.

The same algorithm can have different cases.

blocks.text: Searching is one of the clearest examples of complexity. If you search a list by looking at each element in turn, that is called linear search. In the worst case, linear search may have to inspect every element, so its worst-case work is often described as O of n. That means if the list doubles in size, the worst-case work roughly doubles too.

If the data is arranged as a binary search tree, or if it is sorted and you use a binary search, the search can be much faster. Instead of checking every element, you can discard half of the remaining search space at each step. That gives a much slower-growing complexity, often described as O of log n in the case of binary search on sorted data. The difference between O of n and O of log n is large for big inputs.

items: Linear search may inspect every element in the worst case.
Linear search is often O of n in the worst case.
Binary search on sorted data is much faster.
Binary search is often O of log n.
Organising data can reduce search complexity.

items.meaning: Searching by checking elements one by one until the target is found or the list ends.
A search that repeatedly halves the search space on sorted data.

blocks.text: Sorting is another classic area for complexity analysis. Different sorting methods have different complexities. Some simple methods compare and move elements in a way that leads to roughly n squared work in the worst case. That can be acceptable for small lists, but it becomes slow for larger ones. More efficient sorting methods grow more slowly as the input grows, which is why they are preferred for large data sets.

You do not need to memorise every sorting algorithm in full detail for this syllabus; you need to understand that sorting methods differ in complexity and that more efficient ones grow more slowly. Bubble sort, insertion sort and selection sort are common examples of simpler n squared methods, while more advanced methods are more efficient for large inputs. The syllabus point is that complexity is what lets you compare them.

items: Sorting methods differ in complexity.
Simple sorts are often O of n squared in the worst case.
More efficient sorts grow more slowly.
Complexity helps explain why one sort is preferred for large data.
The same task can have several possible algorithms.

blocks.text: Big-O is useful because it lets you compare algorithms at a high level. If one algorithm is O of 1 and another is O of n, the first is usually better for large inputs, even if the second is faster for tiny inputs due to a small constant. If one is O of n and another is O of n squared, the first will usually win much more dramatically as the input grows. Complexity lets you see these differences before you run the code on huge data.

This is why complexity is often taught alongside searching and sorting. Once you know the growth pattern of each method, you can choose a better one for large inputs. You still have to think about the trade-offs in real life, such as code simplicity and the size of the data you actually have, but complexity gives you the vocabulary to make that choice wisely.

items: Big-O helps compare algorithms by growth.
A smaller Big-O class usually wins for large inputs.
Small inputs can still favour a simpler algorithm.
Complexity supports intelligent choice of method.
Trade-offs still matter in practice.

learn.title: Complexity in the context of the 2027 Computer Science syllabus

blocks.text: In the 2027 ISC Computer Science syllabus, complexity and Big-O are part of the Data Structures and algorithm analysis ideas in Section C. You are expected to understand input size, dominant term, best, average and worst case, and the idea of analysing searching and sorting algorithms using Big-O notation. The emphasis is on the idea, not on formal proofs. You should be able to say what O of 1, O of n and O of n squared mean in words, and why some algorithms grow faster than others.

You are also expected to connect complexity to searching and sorting, so you should be able to explain why linear search is usually O of n and why binary search is usually much better on sorted data. If a question asks about a method you have not met before, the safest approach is to reason from the idea of how much work grows with input size, rather than guessing at a formula you do not know.

items: Know what input size and dominant term mean.
Know best, average and worst case.
Know what O of 1, O of n and O of n squared mean in words.
Be able to talk about searching and sorting complexity.
Reason from growth rather than guessing at formulas.
